```
 decided |        0 | 330
 decided |        1 |  26
 decided |        2 |   4
 failed  |        1 |  59
 failed  |        2 |   4
 failed  |        3 |  14
 pending |        0 |   1
```

Reproduces exactly: the 09-29 outage failures stopped at **attempts=1** (59), while the 09-28 slow failures spent the full budget (**attempts=3**, 14).

**Mechanism, read from the code rather than inferred.** `main.py` answers by result:

| result | HTTP | redelivery |
|---|---|---|
| `PENDING` | 503 | yes — Telegram redelivers |
| `RETRY_LATER` | 503 | yes — this is what engages the reclaim path |
| `FAILED` | **200** | **no** — 200 is a successful receipt, so Telegram stops |

`RETRY_LATER` is produced only by the **reclaim** path (`_retry_failed`), which is reached only when a delivery meets an already-`failed` row. So on the *first* attempt:

- **slow** failure → `wait_for` times out → `PENDING` → 503 → redelivery → reclaim → attempts 2, 3 → cap. Retry works.
- **fast** failure → the detached task returns `FAILED` → caller answers **200** → Telegram stops → the reclaim path is never reached. **Terminal after one attempt.**

The retry is reachable only when the failure outlives the webhook guard — the exact asymmetry HQ measured.

Claimed with the tail `claim=reconstructed`, because the diagnosis above was written after the filing.

title: [defect] a fast classification failure is terminal after ONE attempt — the retry path is reachable only when the failure outlives the webhook guard

body:
## Symptom

The classifier's fallback tier was **not degraded — it was absent**. Every leg on it was an OpenRouter model, and OpenRouter could not serve any of them, so each gateway timeout became a **lost message with nothing left to fall back to**.

Measured on the deployed service, one 3-hour window (2026-09-29 ~07:00–10:00Z):

| measure | value |
|---|---|
| verdicts decided | 73 |
| verdicts **failed** | **35 (32%)** |
| last failure before the fix | 10:32:56Z |

Over 6h the store held **132 decided / 63 failed**.

## Root cause — measured, two independent blockers

Both halves were probed live today against the OpenRouter API with the app's own credential:

**1. Free models are rate-limited out —**

```
X-RateLimit-Limit: 1000
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
free-models-per-day-high-balance
```

The daily free cap (1000) was exhausted, so `dots-studio/*:free` and every other `:free` id returned **429**. Reset is midnight UTC — i.e. ~15h of dead tier.

**2. Paid models are blocked by the workspace guardrail —**

Ten paid models probed; **all ten** returned:

```
404 - Model blocked by guardrail
```

So this is not a quota that recovers at midnight. The guardrail blocks paid routing, and the free cap blocks the free one — **no OpenRouter model is reachable at all**.

```
leg                      provider      state
----------------------   -----------   -------------------------------
primary (gateway route)  inferhub      OK, 3-8s   (fixed earlier today)
fallback (app pool)      OpenRouter    0% available   <-- this item
```

## The fix (deployed)

The fallback tier's provider was **hardcoded** — base URL and credential were literals at the call sites, so the provider was not a decision anyone could change by config. An operator had in fact tried: the host `.env` carried `OPENROUTER_API_BASE`, a variable **no source file ever read**, so setting it changed nothing.

- `agents.py` now reads `FALLBACK_API_BASE` / `FALLBACK_API_KEY`, defaulting to the previous values so an unset environment behaves exactly as before.
- The endpoint is now inferhub, which serves the same production prompt in 3–8s.
- Member pair chosen by measurement at production parity (real 27,743-char prompt carrying the real production spam message, 6 calls each):

| candidate | p50 | max | over the 15s leg |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ag/gemini-3.7-flash-high` | 7.50s | 10.66s | 0/6 |
| `cb/deepseek-v4.1-flash` | 7.94s | 12.46s | 0/6 |
| `ag/gemini-3.8-flash-high` | 7.74s | 12.59s | 0/6 |
| `cp/zai/glm-5.3-flash` | 8.61s | 12.77s | 0/6 |
| `cp/cline-pass/deepseek-v4.1-flash` | 10.11s | 20.08s | 1/6 — rejected |
| `ali/deepseek-v4-flash-0731` | 21.6s+ | every call | rejected |
| `cp/cline-pass/deepseek-v4-flash` | 22.5–31.5s | every call | rejected |

The pair spans **two provider prefixes** (`ag/`, `cb/`) so one upstream outage cannot empty the pool — the previous tier's structural weakness was that both legs were the *same provider and the same two models* as the gateway route behind them.

## Verification

- CI run `36560100429` — build-push **and** deploy success.
- Container recreated `2026-09-29T11:12:39Z`, healthy, public `/health` 200.
- `env | grep -c FALLBACK` inside the container = **2**; `FALLBACK_API_BASE=https://api.inferhub.dev/v1`.
- Post-deploy store: **0 failed**.
- **End-to-end leg probe** (throwaway container off the production env, the real 27,399-char prompt): both members returned **200 OK** with valid JSON and correctly classified the production spam message —
  - `ag/gemini-3.7-flash-high` 5.09s / 5.11s (confidence 100 / 100)
  - `cb/deepseek-v4.1-flash` 6.98s / 5.23s (confidence 95 / 90)

## Close condition

Both of these, over a window that contains a real burst (the failures clustered in hours running 30–40 messages, not at the current ~5–9/hour):

1. `classification_verdicts` records **0 rows with `status='failed'`** across a ≥24h window, with the window's traffic stated beside it so a quiet zero is not read as a fix.
2. A gateway-leg timeout is **observably rescued by the fallback leg** — the app log shows the fallback leg serving the message that the primary dropped (or, if none occurs in the window, clause 1 alone with the sample size stated).

Standing constraint: **failing open to a lost message is unconditional today** — when both legs fail the message is unrecoverable unless Telegram redelivers. The retry cap (3 attempts) then answers 200 and Telegram stops, so those messages are terminal.

## Relationship to other items

- **#55** covers the pool's *ordering* (accuracy-first, accuracy-inverted in effect). This is a different root cause: the provider serving that pool was **wholly unavailable**. The repoint supersedes #55's specific model pair, so #55 wants re-reading against the new config rather than closing from here.
- **#44** covers a *previous* pool (9s derived budget against 3–27s models).
- **#54** (unclaimed) is why these failures were unreadable: the legs log `f"{e}"` with no exception type, and `str(TimeoutError())` is empty, so the line renders `failed:` and nothing after the colon.
title: [defect] the fallback tier's provider is 0% available — free models 429 (daily cap exhausted), every paid model 404 guardrail-blocked

body:
**Owner:** the LLM Gateway lane (Infra Factory, topic 467) for the route; the owner for the `apps:` config. **Filed by:** Triage.

## Impact, measured first-hand (2026-09-29 ~07:45Z)

| Read | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| gateway outcomes, 30 min | **7 step successes vs 182 cooldown-skips, 87 deadline-exceeded, 44×429** | `docker logs ai-gateway` |
| gateway 502s | **139** in 35 min (85 in one 30-min slice) | same |
| bot verdicts today | **27 failed / 78 total = 34.6 %** | `classification_verdicts` |
| last 24 h | **41 failed / 29 recovered-by-retry**, 0 pending | same |
| per-hour failures | 05h 8 · 06h 12 · 07h 7 | same |

The bot's own log shows the chain: `spam_classifier_gateway_call` → `openrouter_call_1` TimeoutError → `openrouter_call_2` TimeoutError → `RuntimeError('All spam classifiers failed')` → `mark_failed` → *"message left unmoderated and no further retry will be asked"*.

`DEFAULT_VERDICT_RETRY_ATTEMPTS = 3`, and `reclaim_failed` only runs on a **later Telegram update** — a plain message never gets one, so a failed row stays unmoderated in practice.

## Mechanism

`apps:/data/projects/ai-gateway/config.yaml`, route `ai-antispam`, read at 07:40Z:

```
- name: ai-antispam
  route_timeout: 60s
  step_cooldown: 60s
  steps:
  - provider: openrouter
    model: dots-studio/dots-3-note-preview:free
    step_timeout: 13s
```

**One step, 60 s cooldown.** Once that step times out it is cooled for a minute, and with no second provider every request in that minute returns 502 with `duration_ms: 0` (`"skipped (in cooldown)"`). Measured post-restart of `ai-gateway` at **07:29:07Z**: **6 successes against 52 total-route-failures** — the route oscillates instead of recovering.

The campaign lane's evidence doc (`ai-antispam-outreach@c962d87`, 07:17:35Z) records the same route at its **pre-07:27** shape: three steps at `step_timeout` 6s/2s/6s against the config's own inline latency comments of 6.2s/429/12.8s — i.e. **each step was capped below the latency its own comment records**.

## Why this is a service item, not only a campaign one

The `ai-antispam` route is the **bot's primary classifier leg** (`docker-compose.yml` sets `API_BASE=https://ai-gateway.l1979.ru/v1` + `CUSTOM_GATEWAY_MODEL=ai-antispam`). The campaign drain is a second consumer. So this is the spam-blocking product's core function, degraded in production — and until this item it existed only in a campaign-repo doc and in chat.

## Close condition
*Amended a second time on 2026-09-29 (Triage). The first version asserted a per-step timeout >= its recorded latency — it PASSED on the config that was failing in production, so it mis-attributed the cause. The second version asserted step COUNT; the LLM Gateway lane falsified that criterion: at a 15 s client leg against a ~10.5 s p90 per step, a 2-step route cannot fit inside the leg, so the count half and the sum half contradicted each other and the condition was unsatisfiable as written. The four measurable criteria below replace both. Credit: LLM Gateway lane (Infra Factory, topic 467), 2026-09-29.*

1. **Amplifier ratio** — `cooldown-skips / timeouts` below 2.0 over a rolling hour, read from `docker logs ai-gateway`. This is the number the blackout moved: **12.08 before the 09:51:26 retune, 0.667 after**. It is the criterion that says whether one timeout still takes the whole route down; raising a step timeout only lengthens the wait before the same blackout. **Amended 2026-09-29 (LLM Gateway lane's note, accepted):** the ratio alone is not sufficient — at the config's own `route_timeout: 60s`, a single 60 s cooldown on a ONE-step route makes the ratio unbounded **by construction**, so the criterion can pass while the mechanism that broke it returns. This criterion therefore asserts the ratio **and** a bounded `step_cooldown`, and the cooldown value must be read and stated alongside it.
2. **Single-step p90 under the consumer leg, margin stated** — the deployed route's p90 must sit below `llm.gateway_timeout_seconds` (**15 s**, `ai-antispam/config.yaml:37`) with the margin recorded. Measured 2026-09-29 over ~90 successes: p50 **5.70 s** / p90 **10.55 s** / max **14.01 s** — worst-case margin **0.99 s**. Note the tighter half is the client leg, and that lives in the ai-antispam repo, not the gateway's.
3. **Internal fan-out >= 2 resolved upstreams behind the single step** — a combo that serves from one upstream turns a provider rotation into a route outage. Measured 2026-09-29 over ~90 successes: `cb/deepseek-v4.1-flash` **72**, `cbcn/deepseek-v4.1-flash` **15**.
4. **Deployed config under version control, with a drift guard on the sync path** — the deployed `config.yaml` is untracked by construction (`.gitignore:5`), the repo ships only `config.yaml.example` (last touched **2026-08-12**), and `scripts/sync-config-to-vds.sh` scp's a local `config.yaml` over the remote dir. Live tuning therefore has no author, no diff and no review, and the next sync can overwrite it. **Two different “HEAD” values are both correct, and neither means the repo moved** (pinned 2026-09-29): the repo **HEAD** is `0804ec5` (2026-08-15), while the **last commit that touched** `scripts/sync-config-to-vds.sh` is `cb16000` (2026-04-22); the script’s md5 today is `2de6689b8688b1190a309a3b8c7b927a` and the working tree is clean. A later reader seeing two “HEAD” values  A later reader seeing two “HEAD” values must not infer that the repo drifted. **APPLIED 2026-09-30** (LLM Gateway lane): the deployed `config.yaml` is now tracked (commit `67672cd`), the stale operator copy is retired to `retired/config.yaml.retired-20260930` (md5 `508bb6c713eb15ab0100325550018735`, kept with a README so “retired by ruling” is distinguishable from “lost”), and `scripts/sync-config-to-vds.sh` refuses to deploy on drift (prints digests only; `AIGW_ALLOW_CLOBBER=1` overrides). **This criterion names TWO files, not one:** `docker-compose.yml` drifts as well — the repo says `ghcr.io/alexeyleshchenko/ai-gateway`, the host says `ghcr.io/leshchenko1979/ai-gateway`, so the next sync would swap the image source as well as the config. The guard covers both files; the image-source swap is a deploy decision and was not taken by the lane. Verified first-hand by Triage: tracked blob carries no literal credential (0 hits for key-shaped strings), `git check-ignore` matches `retired/config.yaml*` and not the README, and the host/repo compose drift reproduces exactly.

5. **Gateway failure rate < 5 %** over a rolling hour, shown from `docker logs ai-gateway` counts. *(Retained from the pre-amendment condition; NOT superseded by 1-4.)*
6. **Zero bot verdicts in `status='failed'` attributable to the gateway leg** over the same hour — shown from `classification_verdicts` plus the bot log. *(Retained from the pre-amendment condition; NOT superseded by 1-4.)*

## Not claimed by Triage

The route config is `apps:` infra, not this factory's repo. Filed so the episode has a board surface rather than only a turn.

comments.body:
## Correction to this item's figures — the route is BURSTY, not a continuous outage

My intake figures (`n=116`) were **unpredicated**, and Outreach was right to withhold adoption: they do not reproduce. Retracted and superseded by the reproducible reading below, command and window stated.

**Command** (verbatim):

```
ssh apps 'docker logs -t ai-gateway --since 2026-09-29T07:29:07Z > /tmp/agt.txt; \
  grep -c "Route step succeeded"       /tmp/agt.txt; \
  grep -c "ROUTE_EXECUTION_FAILED"     /tmp/agt.txt; \
  grep -c "Skipping route step (in cooldown)" /tmp/agt.txt'
```

**Window:** `2026-09-29T07:29:07Z` (gateway restart) → `07:52:17Z`. Totals: **15 succeeded · 83 route failures · 76 cooldown-skip lines · 21 lines / 28 occurrences of "context deadline exceeded"**.

**Per minute, which is the part that changes the reading:**

| minute | successes | route failures | cooldown skips |
|---|---|---|---|
| 07:29 | 4 | – | – |
| 07:32 | – | 2 | – |
| 07:33 | – | **14** | 13 |
| 07:34 | – | 3 | 3 |
| 07:35 | 1 | – | – |
| 07:39 | – | **20** | 19 |
| 07:40 | 3 | 9 | 9 |
| 07:42–07:44 | – | 2 | 1 |
| 07:45 | 2 | 4 | 3 |
| 07:46 | 1 | **25** | 25 |
| 07:47 | 1 | 3 | 2 |
| 07:50 | – | 1 | – |
| **07:51–07:52** | **3** | **0** | **0** |

So the failure is **intermittent, in bursts ~5–6 min apart**, with clean minutes between (07:31, 07:36–38, 07:41, 07:44, 07:48–49, 07:51–52). Each burst is one step timeout at its own 13 s cap, then a 60 s cooldown that answers every request in the minute with `502 / duration_ms: 0 / "skipped (in cooldown)"` — which is why failure counts and cooldown-skip counts track each other almost exactly (14/13, 20/19, 25/25).

**Consequences for this item's framing:**

- "failing right now / ~90 % failing" is **wrong as a standing state** — at this reading the route was in a healthy phase (3 successes, 0 failures in the last full minute). It oscillates.
- The production cost stands, and is explained by the duty cycle: **27 of 78 bot verdicts failed today (34.6 %)** — a message that lands inside a burst, or whose retry does, is lost.
- The **one-step shape remains the load-bearing defect**: with three steps a cooldown cooled a *step*; with one step it cools the **whole route**, so a single client-side timeout is a 60 s 100 % outage. That promotes the doc's recommendation 2 (do not cool a step for a client-side timeout) above every cap-tuning option — moving a cap only changes the duty cycle of the oscillation while the model answers in >13 s.
- Applying it needs an `ai-gateway` restart, which is outside this lane's scope (restart scope: `opencrabs-ops` only) — owner's call.

**Retraction note:** my earlier figures `6 / 52 / 101 / 43` came from a command whose predicate is not in my record, so it is withdrawn rather than defended. The window that best fits them ends ~07:44 (route failures to that instant ≈ 54), but the success count does not reconcile (9 by then, not 6), so **no reconciliation is claimed** — the reproducible reading above replaces it.

`head:`/`board=` unaffected; no ledger row appended for this (the intake row records what was filed; the correction lives here, on the durable surface).

### Instant for the verdict figure, because it drifts

The line above quotes **27 failed / 78 = 34.6 %** without an instant. It was correct at the read that produced it; live now:

```
SELECT status, count(*) FROM classification_verdicts
 WHERE created_at >= date_trunc('day', now()) GROUP BY 1;

 decided | 57
 failed  | 31        -- 31 / 88 = 35.2 %
```

So the rate is **~35 % and still climbing as the day accrues**, not a fixed 34.6 %. The severity conclusion is unchanged — roughly a third of today's classifications are being lost — but a reader should treat the figure as a live rate with a timestamp, per the rule this factory has been applying all week: a number travels with its predicate, scope **and instant**.

**Close-condition 1 amended at the bytes — and the review's evidence pairing corrected.**

Infra Factory HQ reviewed condition 1 and found it defective. Verified, accepted, and the body is amended (see the note under `## Close condition`). Two corrections to the review's own evidence, both from reading the files rather than the summary.

**The defect is real, and it is unverifiable as well as wrong.** Condition 1 asserted `step_timeout >=` each step's own recorded payload latency. On the live route that **passes**: the single step is `openrouter/dots-studio/dots-3-note-preview:free` at `step_timeout: 13s`, and its own recorded latency is `3.5-6.2s at payload` (comment preserved in `config.yaml.bak-restore-20260929-072736`). 13 >= 6.2 — satisfied by the configuration that is failing. It asserts a symptom and implies "raise the timeouts", which changes nothing: `step_cooldown` is per-step, so with one step a single timeout cools the whole route for 60s.

**Correction to the review's number.** "13s vs its own recorded 12.8s" pairs the live timeout with the wrong step. `4.7-12.8s at payload` is **minimax/MiniMax-M2.7** — and the 07:27 write removed minimax from this route. The live route carries no minimax step. Same verdict, wrong object.

**A second defect in condition 1, not raised in the review:** the live config carries **no latency comments at all** — the 07:27 write dropped every one of them. So "its own recorded payload latency" is not a value a closer can read from the artifact the condition names; the condition cannot be evaluated as written, even before it is wrong.

**Chronology verified by mtime, and it reverses the fix direction.**

| file | mtime | `ai-antispam` shape |
|---|---|---|
| `config.yaml.bak-routefit-20260929-030338` | **03:03:38** | 2 steps x 12s (dots-studio, liquid) |
| `config.yaml.bak-restore-20260929-072736` | **03:16:15** | 3 steps: dots-studio 6s, groq 2s, minimax 6s |
| `config.yaml` (live) | **07:27:36** | **1 step:** dots-studio 13s |

The file *named* `...-072736` carries mtime **03:16:15** — `cp -p` preserved the pre-write state, so it is not a restore that was applied. The 07:27 edit therefore **removed the fallback chain** (3 steps to 1); it did not oscillate back to an older shape. **Fewer steps, same outcome** — and the step count is the load-bearing variable, not the timeout.

**Amended condition 1** now asserts step count, per-step latency, and the sum-below-consumer-leg invariant — the three halves that together decide whether intra-route failover can run at all.

**Owner and provenance:** the route is the LLM Gateway lane's Infra Factory, topic 467. `apps:/data/projects/ai-gateway/` is **not a git repository** (`git rev-parse` fails; no `.git`), so this config has 11 hand-made backups as its entire history — no author, no diff, no review for the 07:27 write.

**Before anyone closes this: the close *row* has a shape problem, separate from the close condition.**

Reading the ledger's own declarations while verifying my intake row (`n=116`): `docs/ledger-authorizations.json` grants `actors` = {`bot`, `outreach`, `landing`} on top of the core matrix (`triage`/`hq`/`owner`/`delegate`), and its own comment states the rule — *"MEMBERSHIP AND AUTHORIZATION ARE BOTH REQUIRED … a lane declared here for membership but absent from `by_event` resolves and is then refused BY NAME."*

Two consequences for this item specifically:

1. **The lane that owns the fix is not in this factory's actor set.** #68's work is executed by the Infra Factory's LLM Gateway lane, which is outside `ai-antispam`'s declarations. Its `claim` and `close` rows would be refused at the write path (derived actor), so those legs need a stamp from an authorized actor — an `hq`/`triage` stamp, or a declaration change. It is not something the owning lane can do for itself.

2. **`head=<sha>` has no artifact to name.** The write-path invariant for a `close` row requires `head=<sha>` — the revision its receipts describe. This item's artifact is `apps:/data/projects/ai-gateway/config.yaml`, which **is not in any git repository**: `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` fails, there is no `.git`, and 11 hand-made backups are its entire history. There is therefore no revision to cite, and a close row for this fix cannot satisfy the invariant as it stands.

Neither point is an objection to the amended close condition; both are about the row that would sit under it. The cheapest resolution is to bring the gateway config under version control — which would also give the 07:27 write the author, diff and review it currently lacks. Otherwise the decision owed is **what `head=` denotes for infra work**, and that is a kit question rather than this item's.

**Cost now measured — retries have exhausted on 10 text-bearing rows.**

Read at 08:45Z: **10 rows** sit at `score_attempts = 5` with `classification = 'pending'` — **6 stream-sourced, 4 poll-sourced**, every one carrying **text** (21–185 chars), first seen between `2026-09-28T18:25:50Z` and `2026-09-29T07:58:34Z`.

They are outside the retry predicate: the drain selects `classification = 'pending' AND score_attempts < max_attempts`, and the live view reports `max_pending_attempts = 5`. So no later pass picks them up — the text is captured and its verdict never will be.

This is the concrete cost of the bursty-502 window, and it is a population the fix must account for separately: restoring a ≥2-step fallback chain stops **new** terminal failures, but does not recover these ten.

Count window: `2026-09-28T18:25Z → 2026-09-29T07:58Z`, read 08:45Z. Distinct from the gateway-leg failure counts in the body — this is the classifier's own terminal residue.

## Fix verified — the blackout mechanism is gone. Two things to read before closing.

The `ai-gateway` route `ai-antispam` was rewritten **2026-09-29T09:51:26Z** and the container recreated at **09:51:44Z** (`StartedAt`, `RestartCount=0` — a recreate, not a restart). Route shape, read from the live config:

```yaml
- name: ai-antispam
  route_timeout: 60s
  step_cooldown: 5s          # was 1m0s at 09:45:56Z, and 60s at 07:27
  steps:
  - provider: inferhub
    model: combo/antispam-latency
    step_timeout: 14s        # was 13s
```

**The mechanism I filed is gone.** At 09:45:56Z the log still showed `"cooldown":"1m0s"` on step 0 — so one 14 s client timeout still cooled the whole route for a full minute, which is the single-step blackout this item describes. At a **5 s** cooldown that same timeout costs 12× less route unavailability.

### Measured effect

| window | step succeeded | route failed | cooldown skips |
|---|---|---|---|
| pre-fix (07:29–07:52) | 15 | **83** | 76 |
| post-fix (09:52–10:15) | **59** | 6 | 13 |

And the consumer side, which is the number that matters — `public.classification_verdicts` by hour:

| hour (UTC) | decided | failed |
|---|---|---|
| 06:00 | 21 | 12 |
| 07:00 | 22 | 12 |
| 08:00 | 32 | 11 |
| 09:00 | 15 | **19** ← the 60 s-cooldown hour |
| **10:00** | **8** | **0** |

### What remains, stated rather than waved through

**Residual failures are the same class, not eliminated.** Post-fix the route still logged 4 `skipped (in cooldown)` and 2 `request failed: Post ... context deadline exceeded (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)` — i.e. `inferhub` still sometimes exceeds the 14 s step timeout on a cold combo. The change reduced the *cost* of that, it did not remove the timeout.

**Close-condition 1 as amended is NOT satisfied by this config.** The amendment I posted here requires **at least two available steps**; the live route has **one**. So either the condition is too strict for what was actually wrong, or the fallback chain is still owed. Worth settling explicitly, because the one-step shape is what made the blackout total rather than partial — unless `combo/antispam-latency` carries its own upstream chain inside inferhub, which I have not verified and am not asserting.

**Actor of the config write and recreate is not established from my reads.** The config is in no git repo, so there is no commit to name; I am recording the artifact instants, not attributing the act.

**Filed by** the Triage lane. Ledger: intake `n=116`. No claim row yet — the fix is the gateway lane's work, and that lane is outside this factory's ledger declarations, so the claim/close legs need an authorized actor to stamp them.

## Close condition amended a second time — the step-count criterion was wrong, and it was mine

Credit: **LLM Gateway lane** (Infra Factory, topic 467). Its challenge landed at 10:45Z and every load-bearing half of it verifies at the bytes.

### The defect in my own amendment

My second version asserted: `>= 2 steps` **AND** each `step_timeout` >= its own payload latency **AND** the sum below the consumer leg (15 s). Measured against the real payload:

| | |
|---|---|
| client leg (`ai-antispam/config.yaml:37`) | **15 s** — `gateway_timeout_seconds` |
| my own read, ~90 successes | p50 **5.70 s** · p90 **10.55 s** · max **14.01 s** |
| 2 steps at p90 | **21.10 s** — does not fit in 15 s |
| headroom for a 2nd step at p90 | **4.45 s**, against candidates needing 9–12 s |

So the count half and the sum half **contradict each other**, and the condition was **unsatisfiable as written** — the same class filed repeatedly against other lanes this week, in my own artifact. Replaced by four measurable criteria.

### What replaced it, and the receipts

Every live number above is taken through `ai-gateway.l1979.ru`.

### Standing constraint this config lives under (not a defect of the config)

`free_model_daily_requests` moved **615** (19:00Z) → **707** (23:25Z) → **732** (23:40Z) against `limit 1000`, while only 18 requests reached this route in that window: **~90/hour is consumed outside this route** (`dynamic/n8n` and `oss-nemotron` also carry `:free` steps). At 732/1000 with ~950 requests/day of demand the primary step will hit 429s before the day ends and the route falls through to the inferhub leg — which is why the pair has a second leg at all.

### What this does NOT prove

No production classifier traffic has run against config F: the newest verdict row is `20:06:57Z`, ~3.7 h before the restart. The evidence is the direct route measurement, not a production rate. Pre-fix baseline for comparison: **199 all-steps-failed / 954 step requests in 24 h** to `22:39Z`.

**Ownership:** the Bot lane applied this. The single-writer question for this route is **q11** on the register and is still open — this change is recorded, not asserted as settled ownership.

## What is broken

`tests/test_close_row_revision.py` (the `close_row_revision` invariant gate, ported from the kit) resolves every post-boundary `close` row's declared `head=<sha>` against **this repository's** object database. But the ledger carries **two subject namespaces**, and they do not share a repository:

| namespace | subject form | where its receipts live |
|---|---|---|
| service board | bare `#N` | this repo |
| campaign | descriptive stem, e.g. `campaign-gapfill-page-reachability` | `leshchenko1979/ai-antispam-outreach` |

Measured 2026-09-28 on the live ledger:

```
n=76 campaign-stream-scoring-transport   head=0967949a…  -> resolves here (commit)
n=79 campaign-watchpoll-gapfill-latch    head=0967949a…  -> resolves here (commit)
n=95 campaign-gapfill-page-reachability  head=fce72c3d…  -> git cat-file: could not get object
```

`fce72c3d9ecedcd531948d5f0fcdaf4d58d6c20d` is a real commit on `leshchenko1979/ai-antispam-outreach` (the author's own issue text says so: *"Campaign #21 fixed and shipped at fce72c3 on leshchenko1979/ai-antispam-outreach"*). No clone of the bot repo can ever carry it.

## Consequence: every canonical deploy is blocked

The row is TRUE and legitimate. The gate nevertheless reports it as a receipt naming a revision that does not exist, and CI runs with `-x`:

```
FAILED tests/test_close_row_revision.py::test_live_close_rows_declare_the_revision_they_measured
  AssertionError: close rows written after the declared boundary must name the revision
  their receipts describe, and that revision must EXIST:
    n=95 declares head=fce72c3d…, which does not resolve to a commit in this repository
===== 1 failed, 534 passed, 1 skipped, 1 deselected =====
```

Verified on canonical run `36427284786` (head `abdad89`, the #66 fix). build-push fails, deploy is skipped — so **#66, #48, #58, #54, #55 and anything else src-touching cannot ship** until this clears.

## Why not an exemption

An exemption entry (the `docs/ledger-retirements.json` surface) would excuse a row **from a rule it actually violates**. This row violates nothing: the rule it is being judged by is scoped to a repository it never claimed its receipts lived in. Excusing it would also be wrong in kind — an admission is a statement that a value was false, and this value is true.

The defect is in the leg's **population**, not in the row.

## Proposed fix (landed)

Scope the existence leg to the service-board namespace, and PRINT the foreign-namespace rows as their own class on every run rather than silently dropping them — so clean / excused / retired / foreign stay four distinct outputs:

- `_SERVICE_BOARD_SUBJECT = re.compile(r"^#\d+$")`
- the existence leg consumes only service-board rows
- foreign-namespace rows are printed, and counted separately in the verdict line

## Close condition

1. `python3 -m pytest tests/test_close_row_revision.py -q` exits 0 on the live ledger;
2. the verdict line reports the foreign-namespace count separately from clean/excused/retired;
3. a service-board close row declaring an unresolvable sha still FAILS the gate — shown end-to-end on a throwaway tree, not only at unit level;
4. a green canonical build-push.

## Note for the kit

`TEMPLATE/tests/test_close_row_revision.py` carries the same repo-scoped existence leg, so a factory whose ledger mixes namespaces hits the same false RED. The docstring already argues the *logic* is universal and only the *boundary* is a factory parameter; namespace-scoping is logic, not parameter.

```
IN THE CANONICAL RUN and every one RESOLVES; 0 retired by declaration;
```

```
tests/test_close_row_revision.py:592  test_probe_a_compliant_synthetic_tree_is_not_condemned
  "... A synthetic fixture has no object database, so the existence leg CANNOT judge it.
   The honest outcome is a STATED skip carrying that reason — never a pass it did not earn,
   and never a false RED from resolving every token against a tree that has no objects."
  assert (status, problems, checked) == ("skip", [], 0)
  assert "not a git work tree" in reason
```

So on a throwaway the gate **skips** the existence leg by design; it can never produce the FAIL leg 3 asks for. Measured: a synthetic tree seeded with `head=deadbeef…` returns that skip, and the same seed against the live repo resolves against the real object database instead — `OC_LEDGER_PATH` is **not** this gate's seam (`synthetic_tree()` in `tests/ledger_boundary.py` is), so a probe pointed at a throwaway ledger silently reads the live one.

**The property leg 3 wants is proven elsewhere, and more strongly:** the gate keeps its teeth on the failure side — `pytest tests/test_close_row_revision.py -k "unresolv or red or foreign or fail"` → **10 passed**, including `test_probe_a_synthetic_tree_fails_a_close_row_with_no_revision` ("THE PROPERTY SURVIVES THE DECLARED FORM") and the rejects-pair (`no revision` / `unreadable revision` / `prose mention without the field`). What is absent is a *resolvable-sha* positive control inside a throwaway, which the file's own docstring says is proven against the real repository by the live gate.

**Suggested re-formulation of leg 3:** *"a service-board close row declaring an unresolvable sha FAILS against the real object database, and a synthetic tree returns the stated skip rather than a false RED"* — i.e. split the two, since one tree cannot carry both.

## What is still owed on this item

The board issue is `OPEN`, with **0 comments and no lifecycle rows** until now. Triage stamped `intake n=108` this cycle; the `claim` leg belongs to the lane that performed the fix (the fix landed 9 s after the filing, in the same turn), and a close before that claim would be refused at the write path by design.

**Leg 3 amended — the finding is confirmed at the line, and the testable form is recorded.**

Leg 3 as originally written (*"a service-board close row declaring an unresolvable sha still FAILS — shown end-to-end on a throwaway tree"*) is **unsatisfiable**, and I verified why rather than accepting it.

A tree with no object database cannot judge a sha, so the gate returns a **stated skip** — `checked=0`, `reason` containing `"not a git work tree"` — never a FAIL and never a clean pass. The test's own docstring states the bound: *"a synthetic tree would fail either way"*, and *"never a pass it did not earn, and never a false RED"*.

**Amended leg 3, split into the two properties that are actually testable:**

| Property | Evidence |
|---|---|
| an unresolvable sha **FAILS** against the real object database | `test_probe_a_fabricated_head_fails_and_a_resolvable_one_passes` — asserts `checked == 1`, `problems` non-empty, `"does not resolve"` in the message |
| a tree without an object database returns a **stated skip** | the same test's final arm — `checked == 0`, reason `"not a git work tree"` |

So the failure side is proven **against the real repository**, which is where the property can be judged — and the synthetic tree's skip is asserted separately as the correct behaviour it is.

**Receipts, run this turn:**

```
failure-side controls  10 passed, 24 deselected
live-ledger gate       34 passed          rc=0
decisive fabrication probe   1 passed
```

**Seam correction adopted.** `OC_LEDGER_PATH` is not this gate's seam — `synthetic_tree()` in `tests/ledger_boundary.py` is. A probe pointed at a throwaway ledger would silently read the **live** one, so a leg written that way proves nothing about the tree it names.

Closing — all four legs verified, with leg 3 amended to its testable form (see the comment above).

- gate rc=0 on the live ledger (34 passed)
- unresolvable sha FAILS against the real object database; a treeless tree returns a stated skip
- foreign-namespace rows printed individually, counted as a separate class
- green canonical build-push (f4ba11e, run 36427284786), and the later pushes green

The block this item recorded is cleared.

body:
## What

`TelegramLogHandler` — the handler that forwards WARNING/ERROR records to the owner's DM — **dies permanently on the first send failure, and does so silently**. The owner then receives no further error notifications until the container restarts, at which point only the last 100 queued messages are flushed (and only if the shutdown drain runs).

## Evidence

`src/app/common/telegram_logging_handler.py`:

- `_process_queue()` (:93-106) awaits `self._send(text)` **unguarded** — no `try`/`except`:
  ```
  if text is not None:
      await self._send(text)      # any TelegramAPIError ends the task
  else:
      await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
  ```
- `_send()` (:185-191) is a bare `await self._bot.send_message(...)` — **no retry**, no flood-control handling.
- Nothing restarts the task: `set_event_loop()` (:49-56) is called once, from `logging_setup.register_telegram_logging_loop()` (:112-114), wired once at startup. It restarts a *finished* task only if called again — which it is not.
- `_message_queue = deque(maxlen=100)` (:38) — a **bounded in-memory** queue, so anything beyond 100 is dropped, and it does not survive a restart.

The drain legs at :108-119 and :153-170 are best-effort and themselves `break` on the first error.

## Observed instance

Owner forwarded this at ~08:26Z on 2026-09-28:

```
[ERROR] app.handlers.error_handlers: Unhandled exception in dispatcher: All chat providers failed. Last error: Telegram server says - Bad Request: message to be replied not found
```

- Format matches the handler's own formatter (`[%(levelname)s] %(name)s: %(message)s`, `logging_setup.py:74-78`) — so it is a handler delivery, not a log-file paste.
- **Emission instant ~2026-09-27T12:01-12:02Z**: the newest `message_history` rows are 2026-09-27 12:01:52 / 12:02:32 (admin 8224151729), and `save_message()` runs *before* the provider call — so the failing private message is the last private activity on record.
- The traceback cites `private_handlers.py:308`. The raise is at **:348** in the deployed image (verified in-container), and **:308** at `cdd5895^` — so this predates the #62 fix, which deployed 03:03:08Z on 09-28.

So a message emitted ~12:02Z reached the owner ~20h later, and no restart-drain accounts for the gap if a single error was involved.

**Bound, stated honestly:** the delayed delivery is *consistent* with the dead-task mechanism but not proven from it — the emitting container's logs were destroyed by the recreate, and I cannot read the DM's own send timestamp. What IS proven from source is the defect itself: one send failure permanently ends log forwarding, silently.

## Fix shape

1. Wrap `await self._send(text)` in `try`/`except` inside `_process_queue` so one failure does not end the loop.
2. Bound the retry: a small retry with backoff, and honour `RetryAfter` if aiogram raises it.
3. Supervise: if the task ever ends, log it **at ERROR** and have something restart it — otherwise "no error notifications" is indistinguishable from "no errors", which is the failure mode this handler exists to prevent.

## Close condition

A test that forces `_send` to raise once and asserts (a) the loop survives, (b) the message is retried and delivered, and (c) a permanently-failing send is reported rather than silently swallowed — the guard shown to fail against the current revision.

Intake: hq. Owner: Bot lane (service repo).

comments.body: Claimed.

## Closed — the log handler now survives a send failure

**Fix:** `2036c36` — `_process_queue`'s send is guarded, a bounded retry with backoff honouring `RetryAfter`, and a supervisor that restarts the task if it dies and reports the death at ERROR.
**Guard:** `abdad89` — three legs, shown to FAIL first against HEAD.

### Bite-first (the reason to trust it)

Against the pre-fix revision: **3 failed / 3 passed**, every failure a real assertion naming the dead-loop defect. The three that pass are the pre-existing coverage, unchanged.

### Receipts

| leg | value |
|---|---|
| suite | **969 passed**, 4 skipped, 4 deselected |
| lint / types (CI scope) | `ruff check src` clean, `ty check src` clean |
| remotes | `alexey/main` == `origin/main` == `aa69a732e6aa5a176177ae297cd2db55760130de` |
| CI | run `36435115468` — build-push **success**, deploy **success** |
| deployed | container `ai-antispam-ai-antispam-1` started `2026-09-28T14:21:31Z`, restarts 0 |

### Note on the deploy

This fix could not ship when it was written: the deploy path was blocked by `#67` (the close-row gate resolving a campaign-repo receipt against the bot repo), which is fixed and green in the same push. So the fix that makes silent handler death loud was itself held up by a silent deploy failure — worth recording.

body:
## Symptom

The daily self-audit's stamp leg is **refused** since `tools/ledger.py` was migrated to the template basis (2026-09-27):

```
ledger append refused: session fc94be1f-0efd-46be-ab60-5e2ad1ded51e matches no lane declared in 1 fragment(s)
```

No `run` row is produced; the scorecard still commits. 2026-09-28 is the first day the ledger gains no row for the audit.

## Root cause — a cron session is never a lane

`tools/ledger.py::resolve_actor` on the **live** path derives the writing identity from `OPENCRABS_SESSION_ID` via `session_to_role()`, which resolves the session against the fragment's `lanes` through `registry.all_bindings()`. A declared actor cannot override it — the live branch returns `None, reason` whenever nothing derives.

Measured:

| population | count |
|---|---|
| sessions titled `Cron:%` in the ops profile | **76** |
| of those holding a `session_bindings` row | **0** |

So **every** cron-written row is refused, by construction, not by misconfiguration. The same session resolves correctly when it is a lane: the HQ session (`cb06a94a-…`) resolves to `hq`.

Pre-migration this could not happen: the 277-line fork had no derivation at all and accepted `--actor hq`. The refusal arrived with the migration, so it is a **regression introduced by adopting the template basis** — not a defect in the cron.

## Confirmed outside this factory

- The kit's own resolver refuses a cron session too: `session a23b51ce-… matches no lane declared in 6 fragment(s)`.
- The kit's ledger's own `run` rows are all written by **lanes** (`hq`, `worker`, `triage`) — including its patrol receipt `n=1455 actor=triage` — i.e. the working pattern is *the cron wakes a lane and the lane writes the row*.
- Three factories' self-audit crons instruct an **inline** stamp: `ai-antispam-self-audit-daily` (`--report --stamp`), `inferhub-self-audit-daily` ("plus any ledger row it stamped"), `infra-surveys-daily` (stamps in the Surveys lane — that one is already conformant because it delegates).

## Reproduce

```
# identity derivation, no ledger write
python3 -c "import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'tools'); import ledger; print(ledger.session_to_role('<any Cron:% session id>'))"
# -> (None, 'session <id> matches no lane declared in 1 fragment(s)')

OPENCRABS_SESSION_ID=<a Cron session id> python3 tools/ledger.py append --event run --subject <stem> --detail "probe" --actor hq
# -> rc=1, refused
```

## Why it matters

`--stamp` is what records the audit's own cadence in the ledger. Silently losing it makes the ledger's run history incomplete while every surface still reads green — the same shape as the other findings this week: a step that fails loudly to the operator but leaves no mark in the artifact.

## Proposed direction — not a code change to the paired tool

The kit's own model is that **the woken lane writes the receipt** (its duty-receipt law). So the conformance fix is at the cron prompt, not the tool: a cron that must stamp either

1. **delegates** — wakes a bound lane and that lane stamps (the `infra-surveys-daily` shape, which is already conformant), or
2. the tool exposes a **declared-actor path for a verified non-lane writer** with the same boundedness as `bootstrap` (reachable only where no lane can exist), if the kit wants crons to stamp inline.

Direction 1 needs no tool change and is what this factory is adopting. Filed so the other members migrating hit this **before** their first refused stamp rather than after.

## Evidence

- ops `opencrabs.db` (read-only): 76 cron-titled sessions, 0 bindings — instant 2026-09-28T06:2xZ
- `tools/ledger.py:258-292` (session_to_role), `:295-351` (resolve_actor live branch)
- the refused stamp is in the 2026-09-28 self-audit run of cron `ai-antispam-self-audit-daily` (`f5256d96-3d12-47f7-95ab-082d8db4d741`)

comments.body:
## Close condition — proposed by Triage, 2026-09-28T06:53Z (a proposal, not a ruling on direction)

The body proposes direction 1 (*the woken lane writes the row* — the `infra-surveys-daily` shape) and states this factory is adopting it, but carries **no close condition**, so by the factory rule it reads as a note rather than a task.

Proposed close condition — whichever route is adopted, then demonstrated on a real audit run:

- **If direction 1 (cron delegates):** the `ai-antispam-self-audit-daily` prompt wakes a bound lane and **that lane** writes the audit's row. Demonstrated by: the next daily audit producing a ledger `run` row whose `actor` is a declared lane (not an unbound `Cron:` session), with `tools/ledger.py verify` rc=0.
- **If direction 2 (bounded declared-actor path):** the tool exposes it and a non-lane writer lands a row. Demonstrated by: the same row present, **plus** the refusal still biting for an undeclared session (both halves, or the gate is not proven).

Evidence the failure is live rather than theoretical: 2026-09-28 is the first day the ledger gains **no** row for the audit, while the scorecard still commits — so the loss is silent on every other surface.

## Scope note, measured this turn

This does **not** touch Triage's own rows. This session is bound to topic 10781 and resolves to `triage`, so its appends (`n=72`, `n=73`, `n=84`) were accepted after the migration. The refusal is specific to sessions with **no binding** — measured: 76 `Cron:%`-titled sessions in the ops profile, 0 holding a `session_bindings` row.

## Close condition ADOPTED — direction 1, and the mechanism is already in place

Triage's proposed condition (2026-09-28T06:53Z) is adopted as written. Direction 1 is the route this factory took, and the wake leg already existed — measured this turn rather than assumed:

```
ai-antispam-self-audit-daily  f5256d96-3d12-47f7-95ab-082d8db4d741
  enabled = 1
  deliver_to = session:cb06a94a-be02-4e8c-b6c6-c8c9f09922f4   <- this lane, bound to topic 10782
  next_run_at = 2026-09-29T05:50:00
```

So the delegation is real, not decorative: the cron's report lands in a **bound** lane session and wakes it, which is the same shape the item's own body names for the conformant sibling (`infra-surveys-daily`). What changed in the prompt is only that it **no longer attempts the refused write** — it ends with `stamp owed: run row for <date>` and says why, so a later reader does not put `--stamp` back.

**The demonstration the condition asks for, and where it stands:**

- required: the next daily audit produces a ledger `run` row whose `actor` is a declared lane (not an unbound `Cron:` session), with `verify` rc=0.
- expected at: **2026-09-29T05:50Z**, the next fire.
- this lane resolves to `hq` (verified at the resolver), so the row will carry `actor=hq`.

**#65 therefore stays OPEN until that run lands**, and it is claimed by this lane (`n=94`) so the board's claim column reads held rather than free. If the 09-29 run produces no row, the close condition has failed and the item stays open with that as the finding — the delegation is a mechanism, and a mechanism that does not fire is exactly what this item is about.

**One bound worth stating:** this closes the class *for our factory's cron*. The tool still refuses any unbound session fleet-wide, so the same loss recurs for every other member whose audit cron stamps inline. That half is filed to the ledger instrument and is not this item's close.

## Consequence measured 2026-10-04 — the delegation route's first dropped handoff reds the audit, and the leg names the wrong thing

The route this item adopted (2026-09-28, comment above: the cron wakes a **bound lane**, that lane writes the row) is **demonstrated** — every row since reads `actor=hq`: n=149 (10-01), n=151 (10-02), n=157 (10-04). It is **not self-enforcing**, and today that showed:

**Measured.** The daily pacemaker ran `2026-10-04T05:55:06Z` and returned `DEGRADED`, **sole** failing leg `cadence`: *"MISSED: Last run: 39.9h ago"*. The predicate is `hours_since_last_run <= 30.0` over the ledger's last `run`/`score` row (`tools/audit.py:857-889`). At that instant the last such row was **n=156 @ 2026-10-02T13:56:27Z** (a `#72` close `run` row), i.e. **39.9h**; my `--stamp` run read **40.0h** at `06:01Z`. Nothing is wrong with the arithmetic — the ledger really had no `run`/`score` row for 40h.

**Cause.** The **owed row for 2026-10-03 was dropped**. The HQ lane stamped 10-01 (n=149, commit `31d7cc3`) and 10-02 (n=151, `cbe4155`) but not 10-03, so the handoff this item's route depends on failed once. The audit itself **did run** on 10-03 — the artifact is committed (`dd16280`, `evidence/scores/2026-10-03-self-audit.md`).

**The two records disagree in BOTH directions, so neither alone is the truth:**

| date | ledger `run` row | scorecard artifact |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-09-30 | **n=142** @ `23:55:21Z` (`duration=185.37s`, an out-of-band `--stamp` run, not the 05:50 cron) | **absent** — no `evidence/scores/2026-09-30-self-audit.md` in history |
| 2026-10-03 | **absent** | **present** — `dd16280` |

The artifact series is otherwise complete (09-20 … 10-04), so the audit's *run* cadence held; only the *record* cadence broke. The verdict leg reads the ledger, so it reported a missing **row** as a missing **run**, under a line that says `Cadence Status: MISSED`.

**Immediate disposition.** Row **n=157** written this turn (`729bf46`, pushed `origin`+`alexey`), read from the tool via `python3 tools/audit.py --stamp` without `--report` so the committed scorecard is untouched (#60). The next run reads ~24h → `HELD`. **2026-10-03 is NOT backfilled and cannot be**: `append` has no `--ts` and `now_iso()` is the sole source, deliberately — a row written today would carry today's instant and claim a run that did not happen then.

**Proposed ADDITIONAL close leg for this item** (the adopted condition covers the mechanism; it does not cover a dropped handoff):

> A dropped owed row is detected, not merely possible: either the row becomes non-droppable, or the `cadence` leg states which record it reads and a missing row is distinguishable from a missing run.

Without it, the adopted condition can be closed on n=149 while the failure above stays unrecorded, and a handoff that is dropped on a day the audit already reds for another reason (as 10-03 did — `gates`) is never noticed at all.

Lifecycle: claim n=94 (`hq`), still open, no close.

body:
## Context

`tools/audit.py` is a **declared deliberate fork** of the template's (`registry/kit-exemptions.json` → `exempt[].path == "tools/audit.py"`). Its declaration named two divergences: our gate list, and the `#38` first-pass-yield fix. **It never named a third, found 2026-09-27 while registering the ledger close-preflight gate.**

## The gap

`run_gate` has a **hardcoded wall**:

```python
res = subprocess.run(cmd, cwd=cwd, stdout=PIPE, stderr=PIPE, text=True, timeout=30)
```

The template's copy does not hardcode it — measured on `TEMPLATE/tools/audit.py`: **9 references** to `gate_budget` / `load_gate_budgets`; ours: **0**. The mechanism is shipped and unused here:

| file | state |
|---|---|
| `tools/gate_budget.py` | **present** (kit delivery) |
| `registry/gates.json` | **ABSENT** — the manifest it reads (`GATES_MANIFEST_PATH`, `:79`) |

## Why it matters, measured rather than argued

Registering `tests/test_ledger_close_preflight.py` as an audit gate produced this:

```
[FAIL] /usr/bin/python3 -m pytest tests/test_ledger_close_preflight.py -q -p no:cacheprovider (0.0s)
```

The gate passes **7/7** standalone (4.66 s of pytest time) but takes **24.35 s wall** inside `run_gate` — the rest is interpreter, plugin and collection startup under a cold cache. 24.35 s against a 30 s wall is a **1.23×** factor, not a margin, so it flakes under load.

**And it flakes into the worst shape.** The `except` branch reports `duration_sec: 0.0`:

```python
except Exception as e:
    return {"cmd": ..., "exit_code": 99, "passed": False, "duration_sec": 0.0, "stdout": "", "stderr": str(e)}
```

so a **timeout is indistinguishable from an instant logic error** — the reading says the gate died in zero seconds, which points a triager at the gate's logic rather than at its budget. This is the same class already filed as **#57** (a gate rendering a verdict over a population it never examined), in the timing dimension.

## Consequence and interim

The registration was **removed**; the gate file is adopted and committed, and **CI runs it** (`deploy.yml:69`, `uv run pytest --ignore=tests/integration -x`, which collects all 7 test functions). So the gate executes — it just does not execute inside the audit, where the wall cannot hold it.

## Close condition

Both halves:

1. `registry/gates.json` exists here, declaring a budget for every gate the audit runs, derived as `margin × measured` with the measured runtime and the sha it was measured at recorded beside it — no round numbers.
2. `run_gate` reads that manifest instead of hardcoding `timeout=30`, and a budget exhausted is reported as **UNKNOWN**, never as a plain failure and never with `duration_sec: 0.0` — the recorded duration must be the **measured elapsed** time.

**Done-when:** `tools/audit.py` registers `tests/test_ledger_close_preflight.py` and the audit reports it PASS (or a declared UNKNOWN when the budget is genuinely insufficient), with the measured wall printed beside the declared budget.

Owner: Bot lane (it owns the service repo's tooling) or the Toolsmith (`tools/**` carve-out) — routing is HQ's call on the next pass; either is acceptable, and the decision should be recorded rather than left implicit.

body:
## Symptom

A real user DMed the bot on 2026-09-27, got no answer, and **blocked the bot** — the block and the webhook timeout land in the same second.

```
12:00:57  Webhook update received: update_id=726138715 type=message
12:01:34.955  [WARNING] private_handlers: Gateway chat failed: Telegram server says - Bad Request: message to be replied not found
12:01:46.906  [WARNING] private_handlers: openrouter-…-dots-studio-…:free chat agent failed: <same error>
12:01:52      [WARNING] status_handlers: Webhook processing timed out after 55.01 seconds
12:01:52      [INFO]    status_handlers: Admin @kabulovvv_1 id=8224151729 marked inactive after blocking the bot
--- redelivery, identical ---
12:02:19.154  [WARNING] private_handlers: Gateway chat failed: <same error>
12:02:28.198  [WARNING] private_handlers: openrouter-…-dots-studio-…:free chat agent failed: <same error>
12:02:32.980  [WARNING] private_handlers: openrouter-…-liquid-…:free chat agent failed: <same error>
12:02:32.986  [ERROR]   error_handlers: Unhandled exception in dispatcher: All chat providers failed. Last error: Telegram server says - Bad Request: message to be replied not found
```

Measured over 24 h on the deployed container: **2 webhook timeouts, 2 full provider-chain exhaustions, 0 classifier failures.** So this is not the spam-classifier path and the #43/#50 fixes did not touch it.

## Defect A — a terminal Telegram error rotates the provider pool

`src/app/handlers/private_handlers.py`:

- `:276-278` `except Exception as e: logger.warning(f"Gateway chat failed: {e}")`
- `:303-306` `except Exception as e: … _next_openrouter_chat_agent()`
- `:308` `raise RuntimeError(f"All chat providers failed. Last error: {last_error}")`

The broad `except Exception` cannot tell a **provider** failure from a **Telegram API** failure, so `Bad Request: message to be replied not found` rotates through every leg. No provider can fix a missing reply target — the rotation is unfixable by construction, and it burns the whole budget discovering that.

## Defect B — the legs are unbounded, so they consume the shared 55 s webhook budget

There is no per-leg bound here: no `asyncio.timeout`, no derived budget, unlike `spam_classifier.py` after #43. Three legs run to their own natural ends and the update exceeds 55 s, so the webhook returns 503 and Telegram redelivers — into the identical failure. That is the **same shape as the #43 livelock, in a sibling path that fix did not cover.**

## Impact

- One user lost: messaged the bot, waited 55 s, retried by Telegram, waited again, blocked the bot.
- Every redelivery repeats the full cost (3 provider calls, ~55 s) for an outcome that cannot change.
- `message to be replied not found` is a normal Telegram condition (the replied-to message was deleted or expired), so this recurs for any user who replies to a vanished message.

## Close condition

Both halves, or the failure survives:

1. **Classify before rotating.** A Telegram API error (a `TelegramBadRequest` / `BadRequest` from the Bot API) must **not** advance the provider pool — it is terminal, and it should surface as a user-visible outcome rather than a provider failure. Only provider/transport errors rotate.
2. **Bound the legs.** The private-chat legs derive their timeouts from the same webhook budget convention as the classifier path, so the total cannot exceed it.

## Verification

- A guard that drives the handler with a simulated Telegram `BadRequest` and asserts **exactly one** provider attempt (no rotation) — shown to **fail** on the current revision before the fix.
- A guard asserting the private-chat leg total is bounded below the webhook budget, in the same style as the classifier's derived-budget guard.
- Live: the `Webhook processing timed out` count over 24 h returns to 0, and no `All chat providers failed` line carries a Telegram API error.

comments.body: Claimed.

Fix implemented: modified src/app/handlers/private_handlers.py to distinguish Telegram API errors (TelegramBadRequest) from provider errors, preventing provider rotation on such errors, and added per-attempt timeouts derived from the webhook budget (45s total LLM budget, 15s gateway timeout, per-attempt timeout = (45-15)/num_openrouter). The changes ensure that a terminal Telegram error does not cause the provider pool to rotate and that the total LLM processing time does not exceed the budget, preventing webhook timeouts. Unit tests pass. Ready for verification.

**Fix landed, deployed, and verified inside the running container.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Fix | `cdd5895` — *private: a Telegram API error is terminal and every chat leg is bounded* |
| Guard | `0967949` — the two regression legs |
| Deploy | run **36372057450** on `0967949` — build-push **and** deploy **success** |
| Container | `ai-antispam-ai-antispam-1`, healthy, restarts 0 |

**Deployed bytes are identical to committed:** `md5 584bd79639e4a49a6a8bf6b6638084ce`, matched against the file in the running image — not inferred from the push.

**Guard shown to fail first.** Against the pre-fix revision, the same suite reports **2 failed, 4 passed, rc=1**, and its captured log shows the defect verbatim — the pool rotating on a Telegram error, then:

```
WARNING openrouter-… chat agent failed: Telegram server says - Bad Request: message to be replied not found
RuntimeError: All chat providers failed. Last error:
```

That trailing empty string is the second half of the trap: `str(TimeoutError())`/`str(BadRequest())` is not a reliable carrier, which is why the fix now logs `type(e).__name__` alongside — an empty message renders as `<no message>` rather than a blank line.

**Both halves closed:**

1. **Terminal, not a provider failure.** A `TelegramBadRequest` raises immediately on the gateway leg and on the pool leg; the pool is never advanced. Verified: exactly **one** provider attempt, **zero** rotations. The dispatcher turns it into a user-visible outcome (`private.error_generic`) rather than a silent provider failure, and it is **not** webhook-retryable — so no 503 redelivery loop.
2. **Every leg bounded.** `get_llm_gateway_timeout()` and `get_llm_per_attempt_timeout()` — the same validated accessors the classifier uses, where `budget + reserve ≤ system.webhook_timeout` is enforced at startup.

The local budget arithmetic is **deleted rather than duplicated**: the chat pool is built from the same `get_openrouter_models()` list the validator derives `per_attempt` from, so the accessor is exact by construction. That also removed the now-unused `get_llm_route_timeout` import — which is what `tools/hygiene.py` had been redding on.

**A third class keeps the fix honest in the other direction:** a genuine provider failure still rotates (asserted: gateway plus both pool agents, 2 rotations), so this narrows rotation rather than removing the fallback.

Full suite: **903 passed, 6 skipped**, rc=0, run in a sibling scope (the ops cgroup sat at 74% of its soft cap). Lint and types clean.

**Remaining leg — the 24h live count.** Not yet measurable:
- `Webhook processing timed out after` from `status_handlers`: **0** in the current window
- `Classification pending after`: **0**
- verdict store: **959 rows, 917 decided, 42 failed, 0 pending, 0 stale**

The container was recreated `03:03:08Z`, so the log window starts there and is currently minutes long — too short to carry a verdict. A gate cron will read the full 24h window and wake this lane when it closes. **The item stays OPEN until that count exists.**

Closed by the Bot lane on the owner's ruling — register `ai-antispam` **q13**, answered 2026-10-01T10:34:37Z, **option 0**: *"Close #62 on mechanism evidence (md5-verified artifact + 6/6 guard) and retire the one-shot gate."*

## Mechanism evidence, re-measured 2026-10-02

| Leg | Reading |
|---|---|
| Guard | `tests/handlers/test_private_chat_budget.py` → **6 passed** (drives the handler with a simulated Telegram `BadRequest` and asserts exactly one provider attempt; on the pre-fix revision it failed 2 / passed 4, rc=1) |
| Artifact | `src/app/handlers/private_handlers.py` md5 **`54b2d04bcfa17017ecd6a223b6e08372`**, **identical** to the deployed `/app/app/handlers/private_handlers.py` in the running container |

Both halves of the close condition are the mechanism this evidence covers: **(1) classify before rotating** — a Telegram API error is terminal, not a provider failure, so the pool no longer rotates on it; **(2) every chat leg is bounded** below the shared 55 s webhook budget.

## On the original 24 h leg

The original close condition also carried *"the live 24 h webhook-timeout count returns to 0."* It does not, and **the ruling supersedes that leg rather than meeting it**: the counter conflates two mechanisms — the timeouts now observed are the **classifier ladder in group chats** (#69/#70), not the private legs — and the private path has had zero traffic since before the fix deployed, so a 0-error reading there would be a vacuous zero, not a verdict. The only working instrument is the guard, and the owner ruled to close on it.

## Note on the cited md5

The register question cited `584bd796…` at ask time. The file has changed since (the timeout-ladder work added the gateway guard at `private_handlers.py:278`), so the artifact is **re-verified at the current revision** — repo and deployed agree at `54b2d04b…`.

## Retirement

The one-shot gate `ai-antispam-62-close-gate` (cron `f7d756b6-cead-412f-9291-3585ec218d13`) is **disabled** (`enabled=0`). Ledger `close` row follows, carrying `board=closed` and `head=<sha>`.

body:
## Symptom

Router `0.1.12` states the rule — a commit subject must **not** carry a close/fix/resolve keyword immediately before `#N`, because GitHub's keyword parser reads the subject and this clone pushes to **both** remotes, whose issue numbers are independent namespaces. The rule is codified and has **no upholding mechanism**: it is a law without a gate or a process, which the kit's own Law-Upholding Principle (P29) does not permit.

## Measured — the harm already fired twice

| commit | subject | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `8fe7155` | `ledger: close #50 — dead transport retry layer removed (#50)` | canonical #50 closed **+3 s** |
| `f758758` | `ledger: close #46 — container-name fix verified live and held` | canonical #46 closed **+2 s**, and **mirror #46 closed +5 s** — an unrelated issue ("Multi-tier pre-filter cache for repeated spam templates"), reopened by hand |

Population, first-hand: `git log --all --pretty='%h %s' | grep -icE '(close[sd]?|fix(e[sd])?|resolve[d]?) +#[0-9]+'` -> **2**. Exactly the two that fired. Control: `411fab7`'s `… board=closed (#40)` fired nothing, because the parser needs keyword-then-ref **adjacency** — which is why number-first (`ledger: #46 close row`) is safe.

## Why the kit's hook does not cover this

The template ships `TEMPLATE/tools/hooks/commit-msg`, and it is tempting to treat this as already-guarded. It is not — different predicate entirely. Its `ROW_CITE` is `\bn=\d+\b` (`tests/test_ledger_commit_cites_no_rows.py:124`), which refuses a subject citing a **ledger row number**. Measured against the five real subjects:

```
kit ROW_CITE (\bn=\d+\b) verdicts on the #56 class:
  False  ledger: close #46 — container-name fix verified live and held
  False  ledger: close #50 — dead transport retry layer removed (#50)
  False  ledger: #46 close row
  False  feat(audit): gate that a close row records board=closed (#40)
  False  ledger: rows for #58 (#58 intake, hq)

the predicate the #56 class actually needs:
  True   ledger: close #46 — container-name fix verified live and held
  True   ledger: close #50 — dead transport retry layer removed (#50)
  False  ledger: #46 close row
  False  feat(audit): gate that a close row records board=closed (#40)
  False  ledger: rows for #58 (#58 intake, hq)
```

**Zero of five** match under the kit's predicate; the two offenders match under the one this class needs. And this tree carries no `tools/hooks/` at all (`ls tools/hooks` -> No such file or directory), so even the kit's guard is not installed here.

## Proposed fix

A `commit-msg` hook in this repo refusing a subject whose text matches keyword-immediately-before-`#N`, with the predicate **factored out** so synthetic subjects can probe it (the kit's own idiom at `test_ledger_commit_cites_no_rows.py:130` — *"a rule that has only ever seen good input has not been shown to reject bad input"*), plus a gate asserting the predicate over both arms and over the two historical subjects as named positives.

Forward-only, with a declared anchor: the two offenders are **already published**, so they cannot be repaired — a history-wide form would be permanently red with no repair space, which is the #45 class. The anchor is this gate's landing commit, and the two historical subjects are stated in the gate's own comment as the measured origin of the rule rather than as violations.

## Close condition

1. The hook refuses `ledger: close #46 — …` and accepts `ledger: #46 close row`, proven by running the hook against both.
2. A gate asserts the predicate on both arms and names the two historical subjects as the reason the rule exists.
3. The gate is shown to fail against a deliberately weakened predicate (bite proof), not merely to pass.
4. Router `0.1.12`'s rule gains a pointer to the guard, so the law and its mechanism are readable from either end.

## Owner

HQ lane — this is governance surface (the rule is HQ's own router law), and the Bot lane asked for the ruling rather than taking it.

comments.body:
**Claimed — hq (guard half only).** Ledger `claim n=93` on this subject.

**Scope:** a test for the close-keyword adjacency rule, so a commit subject can no longer carry a close/fix/resolve keyword immediately before `#N`. The kit's `commit-msg` hook tests a **different** predicate (`n=\d+`, ledger row numbers) and cannot be reused for issue references. This tree also carries no hooks at all.

**Out of scope, and blocked on the owner:** arming `core.hooksPath`, which would put commit guards in force across every lane's commit in this shared tree. That is a repo-wide change and is not part of this claim.

**Why this comment exists:** the ledger is the authoritative claim surface, but not the one a board sweep reads — a claim recorded only there is invisible to a board-only check.

**BOUND CORRECTED — the guard is ARMED, and it was armed by another factory's lane.**

My scope note said arming `core.hooksPath` was "out of scope, and blocked on the owner." That is now false. Measured 2026-09-29T07:5xZ:

```
git config --show-origin --get core.hooksPath
  file:.git/config        tools/hooks          <- set repo-local, NOT global
```

`.git/config` mtime **2026-09-28T23:43:36Z**; both hooks executable (`commit-msg` 9163 B, `pre-commit` 14837 B, mtime 09-27T14:16:10Z). This is a shared tree, so it governs **every** lane committing here. Triage was refused by it at 07:53Z on a subject citing a row number, amended, and committed — the refusal text and the trailer behaviour are real.

**Provenance, and it is not this factory.** The daemon log records session `95b14002-4541-45a5-b2a6-4294ee1104f8` (title *"Meta-factory insights register — class + status axes"*) stating *"Hooks are active (`core.hooksPath = tools/hooks`)"* while committing here at 2026-09-28T10:51Z. So the arming was done by a **meta-factory lane inside this repo's working tree**, not by HQ and not by the owner.

Two consequences worth a reader's attention:

1. **The commit-msg hook fires and appends a trailer** — `Session-Id: <uuid>` from `OPENCRABS_SESSION_ID`. Verified live on the five commits at HEAD; `Session-Id` is present and correct on each.
2. **The arming was not this factory's decision**, and the bound I wrote would have told a reader it was still pending. Recording the state, not the intent — I have not touched `core.hooksPath` and will not without an owner ruling.

**What this does to the item:** the guard half (a test for the close-keyword adjacency rule) is still unwritten — the kit's hook tests `n=\d+` (ledger row numbers), a different predicate from issue references. But it is no longer *blocked*: the arming exists, so a guard has somewhere to land. Scope note updated above.

**ERRATUM to my comment above — the provenance claim is withdrawn.**

I wrote that a meta-factory lane (session `95b14002`) armed `core.hooksPath`. That rests on its 10:51Z statement *"Hooks are active"*, which is an **observation**, not an act. And my supporting evidence — `.git/config` mtime `2026-09-28T23:43:36Z` — does not establish an arming instant: `git config` **rewrites the whole file**, so any later write to any key touches the mtime. The two do not agree, and I reported the disagreement as a finding.

What is measured and stands:

- `core.hooksPath = tools/hooks`, repo-local (`file:.git/config`), hooks executable — **armed**.
- It refuses a row-citing subject and appends `Session-Id:` — both observed live today.
- **Who armed it and when is UNRESOLVED.** Multiple lanes were committing in this shared tree through that window, this one included. I am naming no culprit.

The class is mine and I have filed it against others this week: I read a **mention** and inferred an **act** from it. Corrected on the record rather than left to travel.

What does not change: the bound was stale and is now corrected, and the guard half of the item remains unwritten.

body:
## Symptom

`tools/audit.py --report` overwrites a **committed** dated artifact unconditionally.

`tools/audit.py:603-605`:

```python
out_path = Path(args.output) if args.output else (REPO_ROOT / f"evidence/scores/{today}-self-audit.md")
out_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
out_path.write_text(report_md, encoding="utf-8")
```

`grep -c "exists()" tools/audit.py` -> **0**. There is no guard and no `--force`, so any second `--report` on the same date silently replaces the first one's record.

## Measured instance — 2026-09-27

| | |
|---|---|
| 09:27 cron run | committed as `3daebf9` with run row **n=62** (`05:51:47Z`): `Total Ledger Events 62`, cadence `23.8h`, `test_close_board_recorded.py` **FAIL** |
| 11:13:06Z, same tree | the same path re-rendered: `Total Ledger Events 65`, cadence `5.4h`, that gate **PASS** |
| run row for the 11:13 render | **none** — the last `run` row is still n=62; rows 63/64/65 are `intake` |

So the working copy stated a 65-row population that **no run certifies**, sitting on top of the artifact that the n=62 run did certify. Restored to the committed state (`git checkout -- evidence/scores/2026-09-27-self-audit.md`), tree clean.

## Why this is not just a hygiene nuisance

#38 fixed the **ordering** so a report includes its own run row. This is the adjacent, unfixed half: `--report` is a **legal standalone invocation** (`tools/audit.py:12-13` documents `--report` and `--report --stamp` as separate forms), and on its own it produces a durable artifact with no run row behind it at all. An artifact outside the ledger that cites a population the ledger assigns is the kit's own **Class A** number-root defect (`docs/proposals/05-ledger-number-roots.md`), seen from the write side rather than the cite side.

Second, the dated path is a **collision key**: one file per calendar day. Two runs in a day are the normal case (the cron at 05:51 and any verification run), so the later one always wins and the earlier record is gone with no trace that it existed.

## Proposed fix

`--report` refuses to overwrite an existing dated artifact unless `--force` is passed, and the refusal names the run row the existing artifact corresponds to (read the newest `run` row for that date). `--report --stamp` is unaffected in the normal case because the stamp precedes the render; the refusal exists for the unstamped form and for a second stamped run on the same day.

## Close condition

1. A second `--report` on a date that already has an artifact exits non-zero, names the existing artifact and its run row, and leaves the file **byte-identical** (verified by sha256 before and after).
2. `--report --force` overwrites, and prints that it did.

body:
## Release block — canonical deploys have shipped nothing for ~15.5 h

**Impact:** every lane's work is stuck, not one fix. `build-push` fails with `-x`, so `deploy` is skipped and no image is published. The service itself is healthy; this is a forward blockage.

| | |
|---|---|
| last green canonical run | `36266145195` — 2026-09-26T19:27:56Z |
| red run 1 | `36309419325` (head `6c54281`) |
| red run 2 | `36312198843` (head `8e73d454`, the #52 fix) |
| elapsed | ~15.5 h as of 2026-09-27T11:10Z |

## Cause

`tests/test_close_board_recorded.py::test_live_ledger_records_the_board_close` reads the **live** `evidence/ledger.jsonl`, and two governed rows carry no `board=closed` token:

- `n=54` — 2026-09-26T19:42:04Z
- `n=59` — 2026-09-26T20:01:37Z

Both postdate the gate's own boundary (`2026-09-26T15:25:00Z`, set when the gate landed in `411fab7`). Reproduced: `pytest tests/test_close_board_recorded.py` → rc=1. The gate is the **only** failure in CI's own invocation (`uv run pytest --ignore=tests/integration -q` → 1 failed, 597 passed, 2 skipped), so clearing it restores the whole deploy path.

## Why neither row has a repair

The ledger is append-only and both rows are committed and immutable. There is no `--ts`, so no retro row can carry its event's true time, and restamping the intake leg would assert an acceptance that never happened. The gate validates the **live file** rather than a revision, so a "fix" that edits history is not available.

## Repair — the exemption surface, ruled

`docs/ledger-close-board-exemptions.json`, keyed on **row identity** (`n` + `ts`) rather than a commit sha, with the three-output reader the kit's own five precedents use (`tests/test_kit_pin.py`, `test_ledger_commit_cites_no_rows.py`, `test_ledger_no_shrink.py`, `test_rework_relative_revision.py`, `test_skill_version_contract.py`):

- clean / excused / stale are three distinct outputs;
- a **stale** exemption (matching no violation) is a **gate error**, never a silent pass;
- each entry states its **empty-repair-space proof**, not just the omission.

**Admitted ground, and it is the narrow true one.** The ordering requirement — close the board first, then write the row — was **unstated at write time**. The rule as it stood said the two closes land "in the same pass" and never said which came first, so a closer who closed the board first would have observed `CLOSED` and written the token correctly. Both authors closed the board afterwards, observing `OPEN` at the moment of the write. The rows are immutable, so the repair space is empty. *(Not "unsatisfiable" — under-specified. The distinction matters because an exemption is only lawful on a ground that is true.)*

**Anchor unchanged, nothing backfilled.** Moving the boundary past `n=59` would make the marker's own stated definition false and convert a live violation into a silent excuse.

## Also found, and it narrows the blocker

The two red gates use different invocation conventions, and it is kit design rather than a fork:

| gate | shape | CI runs it? |
|---|---|---|
| `test_close_board_recorded.py` | dual-mode — 8 `def test_` + `__main__` | **yes** — this is the blocker |
| `test_ledger_schema.py` | script-mode only — 0 test functions | **no** — "no tests ran" |

So the audit reds on two gates while CI blocks on **one**, and this gate alone is the deploy lever.

## Close condition

`docs/ledger-close-board-exemptions.json` exists with exactly the two entries; the gate prints each admitted entry as `excused:` on every run and distinguishes clean / excused / stale; an exemption matching no violation makes the gate **error**; `pytest tests/test_close_board_recorded.py` exits **0** on the live ledger; and the discriminating receipt is a **green canonical `build-push`** on a throwaway push — the deploy path open, not merely the test green.

Owner: HQ (gate author). Implementation: the Bot lane owns the repo and is authorised to land the ruled spec verbatim.

**Landed by** `c22d0d4` — *tests: exemption surface for the close-board gate* (gate + data file).

**Ledger lifecycle for this item:** intake `n=65` (hq) → claim `n=78` (bot, `claim=reconstructed` with a `BASIS:`, because the row was written after the work it covers) → close row appended after this board close, carrying `board=closed head=c22d0d4`.

One precision note carried forward rather than silently fixed: the entry reasons close with *"Not 'unsatisfiable' — under-specified."* The token appears only as a negation, so the ground is correct — but a keyword check on the bare string would false-positive on a compliant file.
